(for the interested -- we now symlink the 'base' and 'recommended' packages into a pseudo-system library, and force the R session to view that pseudo-system library as the true system library, isolating us from other packages installed in the system library.)

Cheers,
Kevin

messages.subject_clean: How does packrat determine package dependencies?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Brian,

Right now, Packrat only captures package names, not versions, from the DESCRIPTION file. If it pulled jsonlite 0.9.7, I imagine it is because you currently have that version installed in the user library -- packrat will default to matching package versions in the user library when first initializing a project (just so that states are 'matched').

You can use `old.packages()` and `update.packages()` to see if you have any CRAN packages that need updates; we're also trying to implement something similar for packages living on GitHub / other repositories.

Thanks,
Kevin

messages.subject_clean: Essential packages for packrat/package dev workflow in system library cause "unexpected" warning
messages.body_plain:
Hi Janko,

I think we need to improve the language we use here, since this has been a common point of confusion But to explain the situation, there are typically two places where packages will live (two libraries):

1. The 'system' library, as specified by .Library -- for example, on my system, I see:

> .Library
[1] "/Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Resources/library"

This will likely point to a library alongside your R installation on Windows. You can see the packages within here with:

> installed.packages(.Library)

You will see a large set of R packages that come bundled with R.

Then there is the 'user' library, which is found with .libPaths(). For example, I see:

> .libPaths()
[1] "/Users/kevin/Library/R/3.2/library"
[2] "/Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Versions/3.2/Resources/library"

That first library is my 'user' library, the second is the system library. These are the places where packages are looked up when e.g. 'library(stats)' is called.

Packrat currently requires (for Windows) that only 'base' packages live within the 'system' library (because otherwise, we break isolation as those packages you see in the warning are universally available across projects). We have some migration scripts for moving any user packages in that system library to a user library, but we are also investigating whether we can avoid this problem altogether.

You can try:

    packrat:::migrate_packages()

to clean up the system library (it will re-install those packages in a user library), or wait for us to investigate this.

Thanks,
Kevin

messages.subject: Re: ignoring imported data packages
messages.body_plain:
Sorry, there isn't a mechanism for this in packrat. An alternative:

Turn on the global cache. This installs packages into one 'global' area, and symlinks them into projects as needed, so that even if you have multiple projects using (some version of) dplyr, they will all grab the same (single) version from the cache. Do this with:

    packrat::set_opts(use.cache = TRUE)

then run 'packrat::snapshot()' and 'packrat::restore()' to migrate any project packages to the cache. Note that this is still a bit experimental so you may hit some bugs -- please let us know if you do. So even if you get 'lahman' and 'hflights', they only have to exist once on your system, yet you will still get the same isolation that Packrat provides. (each unique version of a package gets its own entry in the cache)

Cheers,
Kevin
